name: Acsah (Caleb's daughter)
title: Caleb's courageous daughter
summary: Aksah was the daughter of Caleb, a Kenizzite incorporated into the tribe of Judah, who was among the twelve spies sent to explore Canaan. She was given as wife to Othniel, son of Kenaz, after his conquest of the city Kiriath-Sepher (Debir). Aksah showed remarkable initiative and practical wisdom when she dismounted from her donkey and asked her father for water springs beyond the dry Negev land she had already been granted. Caleb granted her request and gave her both the upper and lower springs—a gift of vital importance for survival in the arid southern landscape. By taking the initiative and speaking on her own behalf in a patriarchal context, Aksah emerges as a distinct and capable female figure in Israel's conquest narratives. Her husband Othniel later became Israel's first judge.

keyEvents.title: Caleb offers Acsah's hand in marriage
keyEvents.description: Caleb promised to give his daughter Acsah to whoever captured the city of Kiriath-sepher (Debir), a Canaanite city in the hill country of Judah. The offer linked military bravery with a marital alliance and land distribution.

keyEvents.title: Married to Othniel
keyEvents.description: Othniel, son of Kenaz—Caleb's younger brother or close relative—captured Kiriath-sepher and received Acsah as his wife as promised. The marriage strengthened the bond between two significant Kenizzite families.

keyEvents.title: Acsah asks for water springs
keyEvents.description: When Achsah came to Othniel, she took the initiative to ask her father for a blessing. She dismounted from her donkey and asked Caleb for water springs for the dry Negev land she had received. Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs—a gift of great practical significance for livelihood in the arid southern landscape.

keyEvents.title: The Account Repeated in the Book of Judges
keyEvents.description: The story of Achsah's marriage to Othniel and her request for water springs is retold in the Book of Judges, underscoring the event's importance in Israel's early conquest history and the allocation of territories among the tribes in Canaan.

footnotes.text: The name Achsah (Hebrew: עַכְסָה, 'Akhsah') likely means 'ankle chain' or 'anklet.' This may indicate that she was regarded as valuable and beautiful.

Kiriath-sepher (also called Debir) was a Canaanite city in the hill country of Judah. Archaeologists have proposed Tell Beit Mirsim or Khirbet Rabud as possible locations for this city. Excavations at Khirbet Rabud have uncovered remains from the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age, which align with the biblical chronology.

Achsah's request for water springs (Hebrew: גֻּלֹּת מַיִם, 'gullot mayim') demonstrates practical wisdom in a dry landscape. The upper and lower springs ensured a year-round water supply and were crucial for agriculture in the Negev region.

The account of Achsah appears both in Joshua 15:16–19 and Judges 1:12–15. This parallel tradition is an important example of how shared source material was preserved in two different literary contexts—one focusing on land distribution, the other on the tribes' efforts to occupy their allotted territories.
Othniel son of Kenaz, Achsah's husband, later became Israel's first judge (Judg 3:7–11). The marriage between Achsah and Othniel thus connected two significant figures in the conquest tradition.

In rabbinic tradition (Talmud Bavli, Temurah 16a), Othniel is identified as a man of great learning—he is said to have restored forgotten halachot after Moses' death. Achsah's role as his wife is thereby given added weight as a figure of wisdom in Israelite tradition.

Achsah's bold request to her father is remarkable in a patriarchal context. She is one of the few women in the Joshua narrative who acts actively and speaks on her own behalf, giving her a unique position among women in the conquest stories.

The verb used when Achsah 'dismounted' from her donkey (Hebrew: וַתִּצְנַח, 'vattitsnach') is debated among scholars. Some interpret it as meaning she jumped or slid off the donkey as a sign of respect or to signal that she had a request to make.
